title: Introduction — What Is the Book of Enoch?
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Its history and relationship to Scripture
description: An introduction to the Book of Enoch (1 Enoch), exploring its origins, its place among the pseudepigrapha, and the principles by which Reformed Christians should approach this ancient Jewish text. We examine its historical significance, its influence on Second Temple Judaism, and its relationship to the canonical Scriptures.

title: The Watchers (1 Enoch 1-5)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Angels who left their proper domain
description: An examination of the opening chapters of 1 Enoch, which present a grand theophany and introduce the concept of the Watchers — angelic beings appointed to watch over humanity. We explore the cosmic framework of God's sovereignty, the obedience of creation contrasted with human rebellion, and the biblical roots of the Watcher tradition in Daniel and Jude.

title: The Fall of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6-16)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — The sons of God and daughters of men
description: A detailed study of the fall of the Watchers in 1 Enoch chapters 6-16, examining their pact on Mount Hermon, the forbidden knowledge they taught humanity, the Nephilim, and God's judgment upon the fallen angels. We connect this narrative to Genesis 6, 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6, and the Puritan theology of Thomas Goodwin on divine grace.

title: Enoch's Journeys (1 Enoch 17-36)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Visions of heaven, hell, and cosmic geography
description: A study of Enoch's cosmic journeys through the furthest reaches of creation, examining the places of judgment, the compartments of Sheol, the tree of life, and the storehouses of the elements. We connect these visions to the biblical tradition of heavenly ascent found in Isaiah, Ezekiel, Paul, and Revelation.

title: The Parables of Enoch (1 Enoch 37-44)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — The Son of Man and messianic prophecy
description: An examination of the Parables (Similitudes) of Enoch, focusing on the figure of the Son of Man — a preexistent, heavenly messianic figure who judges the wicked and vindicates the righteous. We explore the connections to Daniel 7, the Gospels, and the Pauline epistles, and consider how this tradition illuminates New Testament Christology.

title: The Son of Man (1 Enoch 45-57)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Christ-like figure in Jewish apocalyptic
description: A continuation of our study of the Son of Man in the Parables of Enoch, examining the throne of glory, the judgment of the wicked, the preexistence of the Elect One, and the overthrow of earthly kingdoms. We trace the parallels with Isaiah, Daniel, Matthew, Colossians, and Philippians, and reflect on John Owen's theology of progressive messianic revelation.

title: The Book of Luminaries (1 Enoch 72-82)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Cosmic order and God's design
description: A study of the oldest section of 1 Enoch — the Book of Luminaries — which presents a detailed account of the movements of the sun, moon, and stars. We examine the theological message of cosmic order as testimony to God's faithfulness, the connection between natural law and covenant promise, and the Puritan emphasis on divine design in creation.

title: The Dream Visions (1 Enoch 83-90)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Animal Apocalypse and Israel's history
description: An examination of the Dream Visions of 1 Enoch, focusing on the Animal Apocalypse — a remarkable allegorical retelling of Israel's history from Adam to the messianic age. We explore the symbolism of bulls, sheep, and predators, the theology of angelic shepherds, divine sovereignty through morally accountable agents, and the vision of cosmic restoration.

title: The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91-105)
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — Woes, blessings, and the final judgment
description: A study of the Epistle of Enoch, examining its moral exhortation, the Apocalypse of Weeks, the woes against the wicked, the blessings for the righteous, and the problem of theodicy. We connect these themes to the canonical wisdom literature, the Sermon on the Mount, and the Puritan theology of intergenerational faithfulness.

title: Jude and Enoch
subtitle: The Book of Enoch — How the New Testament references Enoch (Jude 14-15)
description: Our concluding study examines the direct quotation of 1 Enoch in Jude 14-15, the theological implications of apostolic use of extra-canonical sources, and the broader connections between Enochic traditions and the New Testament. We reflect on John Owen's principles of canonicity and the proper use of ancient literature in Christian study.
